clue.text: Sweet gents maybe heading up north of Cork?

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word heading up is read from the bottom, so the toilet word runs backwards
in a down entry, north of means placed above, so the toilet piece comes before the cork piece

blocks.note: the gents is a men's toilet, and bog is British slang for a toilet
a cork is a stopper for a bottle; the capital letter hides it behind the Irish city

explanation.surface: A man from the gents heads north of the city of Cork in search of something sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: Cork looks like the Irish city but is just a bottle stopper, and gents maybe is a toilet, hinted by example; bog is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A gobstopper is a large, hard British candy that lasts a long time in the mouth, so it is a kind of sweet.

clue.text: Idiots beginning to startle judge

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of startle is kept

blocks.note: asses are fools or idiots
the opening letter of startle

explanation.surface: Fools set about startling a judge in court.
explanation.walkthrough: Judge reads as a noun on the surface but works as a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to evaluate or weigh something up, which is what judging it means as a verb.

clue.text: Collaborator with police popular earlier

blocks.note: something popular is in, as in fashionable
former means earlier, previous

explanation.surface: A trendy former accomplice has switched sides to work with the police.
explanation.walkthrough: Popular = IN is a standard crossword equivalence, as in 'the in thing'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informer secretly supplies information to the authorities, a person who cooperates with detectives against others.

clue.text: Magical Bronte language

indicators.note: magic transforms things, so the novelist's surname is conjured into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the surname of the literary sisters, used as letters

explanation.surface: A spellbinding style of prose from one of the Bronte sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bronte sisters were the Victorian novelists Charlotte, Emily and Anne; only the six letters of their surname matter here.
explanation.definitionFit: Breton is the Celtic tongue spoken in Brittany, in north-west France.

clue.text: Wild animals making mistakes crossing one river

indicators.note: to cross is to span, so the mistakes word stretches across and encloses one river

blocks.note: gaffes are blunders or mistakes
the Roman numeral for one
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Wild animals blundering as they try to get across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: I and R go together inside GAFFES, just after the G.
explanation.definitionFit: Giraffes are long-necked African mammals living on the savanna, examples of creatures found untamed.

clue.text: Competent-sounding son of leading man

indicators.note: sounding means the word for competent is heard rather than seen, so only its pronunciation counts

blocks.note: able means competent, and the name is pronounced the same way

explanation.surface: A leading actor's son sounds like a capable chap.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading man is not an actor but Adam, the first man in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, Abel was the second child of Adam and Eve, killed by his brother Cain.

clue.text: Visits doctor before work with something bad

blocks.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor
an op, short for opus, is a musical work
a sin is a wrongdoing, something bad

explanation.surface: Someone calls on the doctor before going to work with something wrong with them.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a patient's visit, but the doctor only supplies DR; the break between pieces does not match the break in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop in on someone is to pay them a casual, unannounced call, which is paying a visit.

clue.text: Bizarre citadel overlooking German city’s shops

indicators.note: bizarre means odd, so the fortress word appears in a strange order
in a down entry, overlooking means sitting above, so the fortress letters come before the German city

blocks.note: a fortress, used here only for its letters
Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr; the possessive adds the S

explanation.surface: A strange fortress looming over the shopping streets of a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram covers only the fortress word; ESSEN'S then follows, and shops is the definition rather than more wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicatessens are stores selling prepared foods, cooked meats and cheeses, so they are a kind of retail outlet.

clue.text: Sign of hope in part of London led by artist

indicators.note: to be led by something is to have it in front, so the painter goes first

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the stock crossword artist
used as it stands
Bow is a district in East London

explanation.surface: A hopeful sign appearing over a London district, painted by an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is an area of East London, home of the Bow Bells that define a cockney.
explanation.definitionFit: After the Flood, God set a rainbow in the sky as a promise, so it stands for optimism and brighter times.

clue.text: Hans now dashes out to have a comfort break?

indicators.note: out means disordered or wrong, so the letters of the first three words are rearranged

blocks.note: a name plus two words, used only for their thirteen letters

explanation.surface: Hans hurries off to go to the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the euphemism: 'wash one's hands' is a polite way of saying one needs the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are genteel euphemisms for visiting the lavatory, so each stands in for the other.

clue.text: Hoodlum grabs cricket trophy and behaves aggressively

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so the thug word holds the trophy inside it

blocks.note: a lout is a rough, uncouth young man
the Ashes is the trophy contested in England-Australia Test cricket

explanation.surface: A thug snatches a cricket trophy and turns violent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the famous cricket series between England and Australia, played for a tiny urn.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash out is to attack suddenly, physically or verbally, which is acting with hostility.

clue.text: Book finally appearing? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means falling just short, so the phrase stops one letter before its end

blocks.note: something finally appearing has come at last

explanation.surface: A book finally comes out, or almost does.
explanation.walkthrough: AT LAST loses its final T.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound volume of maps, a particular kind of reference work.

clue.text: Puzzles like this one not half making you angry

indicators.note: not half means only half is kept, so the second half of the puzzle word goes

blocks.note: the thing you are solving is a crossword puzzle

explanation.surface: A solver complains that puzzles like this one drive them mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Not half also means 'very much' in British slang, which the surface leans on; here it just keeps the first five of ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross is an everyday British word for annoyed or irritated, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Policy document that is easy to see? Nothing to it!

indicators.note: adding something to it means appending it after the easy-to-see word

blocks.note: manifest means obvious, plain to see
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A party's policy document is so transparent there is nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface jeers that there is 'nothing to it', but that phrase just tacks O onto the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A manifesto is a published statement of a political party's aims and intentions, typically before an election.

clue.text: Name of city once recollected in a grand list

indicators.note: re-collected means gathered up again, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

blocks.note: three words used only for their ten letters

explanation.surface: A former city name recalled among a long list of place names.
explanation.walkthrough: Recollected reads as 'remembered' but splits as re-collected.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalingrad was the Soviet-era title of Volgograd, renamed in 1961, so it is a former label for that Russian city.

clue.text: Worker in bar to become thin — reduced stones within!

indicators.note: within places the stones piece inside the word for becoming thin

blocks.note: to taper is to narrow gradually
stones reduced to their abbreviation, ST, the British unit of body weight

explanation.surface: A barman slims down, having shed several stones.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of body weight (14 pounds), abbreviated ST, which suits the slimming surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapster is an old word for someone who draws and serves beer from the tap in a pub.

clue.text: Movement of football player? Ref rants if it’s foul

indicators.note: foul means bad or corrupted, so the referee's words are spoilt into a new order

blocks.note: two words used only for their eight letters

explanation.surface: A referee rages at a foul during a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: Foul looks like a football offence but works as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A transfer is the move of a soccer professional from one club to another, usually for a fee.

clue.text: Illness making one conk out when traversing oceans?

indicators.note: to traverse is to stretch across, so the dying word spans the oceans and holds them inside

blocks.note: to conk out is slang for to die, with one as the person who does it
oceans are seas

explanation.surface: A sickness that kills people on long ocean voyages, such as scurvy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests sailors dying at sea; the seas simply sit inside DIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease is a sickness or disorder of the body, a direct synonym for being ill.

clue.text: Cad, revolting man, leading church? Look out now!

indicators.note: leading means going in front, so the rebel comes before the church

blocks.note: a dog is a contemptible man, a cad
Wat Tyler led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, so he is a man who revolted
CH is the usual abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A warning cry about a disgusting cad who has taken charge of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Revolting reads as 'disgusting' but means 'rebelling': Wat Tyler was the leader of the English Peasants' Revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogwatch is one of the two short evening shifts of duty aboard ship, a spell of lookout happening at a particular time.

clue.text: Carol, having eaten rich food, is yelling

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside, so the carol word takes the rich food in

blocks.note: to carol is to sing joyfully
cream is a rich dairy food

explanation.surface: Carol, a woman who has overindulged, is shouting.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol looks like a name but is the verb to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Screaming and yelling both mean shouting loudly, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Anne is unstable, mad

indicators.note: unstable means not holding steady, so the name and verb do not keep their order

blocks.note: a name and a verb used only for their six letters

explanation.surface: Anne is unstable and has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Unstable does double duty on the surface as a description of Anne, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Insane and mad both describe someone who has lost their reason, a direct synonym pair.

clue.text: Worker stealing poet’s gold

indicators.note: stealing takes something away, so the precious metal is removed from the poet

blocks.note: Oliver Goldsmith was an Irish poet and playwright of the 18th century
used as it stands; these letters are the ones taken away

explanation.surface: A labourer pockets a poet's gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Oliver Goldsmith, author of The Deserted Village; take GOLD out of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A smith is a metalworker, such as a blacksmith, a person who labours at a trade.

clue.text: Only chap losing heart is unsmiling

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter, and losing it removes that letter from chap

blocks.note: sole means only, as in sole survivor
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: The only man who has lost heart is not smiling.
explanation.walkthrough: MAN loses its middle letter, A, to become MN.
explanation.definitionFit: Solemn means grave and serious in manner, describing a face showing no amusement.

clue.text: Get on when provided with a coach?

definitions.text: Get on when provided with a coach?

blocks.clueFragment: Get on when provided with a coach?
blocks.note: surface reading: getting along or making progress once you have a personal trainer

blocks.clueFragment: Get on when provided with a coach?
blocks.note: setter's reading: board a vehicle; the prefix meaning provide with (as in embolden) is attached to a word for a coach

explanation.walkthrough: Coach suggests a trainer, and get on suggests succeeding; in fact it is climbing aboard a road vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Embus is a mainly military verb meaning to put troops onto, or climb into, a motor vehicle for transport.

clue.text: Flowing water to be hot

blocks.note: the Scottish and northern English word for a small stream
the verb for giving off heat or being on fire

explanation.walkthrough: A burn is the Scottish word for a brook, which surprises readers who know only the fire sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Burn is both a Scottish word for a brook and a verb for blazing with heat, two unrelated senses.

clue.text: Mechanical tool tangles up when broken

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the preceding letters are put back together differently

blocks.note: two words used only for their nine letters

explanation.surface: A machine that jams and tangles when it breaks down.
explanation.walkthrough: Tangles up already hints at disorder, but the signal to rearrange is when broken.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple gun is a handheld device that drives metal fasteners into wood or board, an example of a mechanical implement.

clue.text: Boy harbours desire to be a manual operator

indicators.note: to harbour is to shelter within, so the boy word holds the desire inside

blocks.note: a son is a boy
an urge is a strong desire

explanation.surface: A boy secretly longs to become a machine operator.
explanation.walkthrough: Manual operator suggests someone running machinery by hand; a surgeon operates, with their hands. The word comes from Greek for handwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon is a doctor who performs operations, working by hand on the patient; hence a cryptic hand-worker who operates.

clue.text: They come together on musical stage, giving signs to the audience

definitions.text: They come together on musical stage

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word for signs counts only as it is heard

blocks.note: symbols are signs, and the percussion word is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: Performers gather on stage in a musical and signal to the watching audience.
explanation.walkthrough: They come together describes the brass plates being clashed, not a cast assembling.
explanation.definitionFit: Cymbals are percussion discs played by striking one against the other in an orchestra or band.
